content: Forceps are handheld, hinged instruments designed for grasping and holding objects. They are particularly useful when fingers are too large to handle small objects or when multiple objects need to be held simultaneously while the hands are occupied with performing a task. The term forceps is predominantly used in the medical field, whereas outside of medicine, similar tools are often referred to as tweezers, tongs, pliers, clips, or clamps. Notably, the singular and plural forms of forceps are the same, and it is never referred to as forcep or a pair of forceps, unlike scissors. The word originates from the Latin term forca, meaning a snare or trap. Mechanically, forceps operate on the principle of the lever to grasp and apply pressure. Surgical forceps are typically made of high-grade carbon steel, which ensures durability and the ability to withstand repeated sterilization in high-temperature autoclaves. Forceps intended for single-use are often made of plastic. There are two primary types of forceps: non-locking (commonly called thumb forceps or pick-ups) and locking forceps. Both types are available in numerous specialized forms for various applications. Non-locking forceps can be further divided into two basic designs: those hinged at one end, away from the grasping end (colloquially referred to as tweezers, though medical professionals rarely use this term), and those hinged in the middle, resembling scissors. Unlike scissors, however, forceps meet at flat, grasping surfaces rather than interposing blades. Locking forceps are almost always hinged in the middle, though some designs place the hinge closer to the grasping end. Locking forceps use various mechanisms to secure the grasping surfaces in a closed position, allowing for manipulation or independent clamping, grasping, or holding of objects. Thumb Forceps Thumb forceps are typically held between the thumb and two or three fingers of one hand, with the top end resting on the anatomical snuffbox at the base of the thumb and index finger. Spring tension at one end keeps the grasping ends apart until pressure is applied. This design allows for quick and easy grasping of small objects or tissue, enabling the user to move and release them or to hold tissue with variable pressure. Thumb forceps are commonly used to hold tissue in place during suturing, to gently move tissues aside during exploratory surgery, and to handle dressings or draping without using the hands or fingers. Thumb forceps may have smooth tips, cross-hatched tips, or serrated tips (often referred to as mouse's teeth). Common tooth arrangements include 1x2 (two teeth on one side meshing with a single tooth on the other), 7x7, and 9x9. Serrated forceps are used on tissue because, counterintuitively, teeth cause less damage to tissue than smooth surfaces by requiring less overall pressure to grasp. Smooth or cross-hatched forceps are used for tasks such as moving dressings or removing sutures. Adson Tissue Forceps Adson tissue forceps often feature a 1x2 mouse's teeth arrangement on the lower tip, which is specifically designed for handling delicate tissues. Locking Forceps Locking forceps, sometimes referred to as clamps, are used to grasp and hold objects or tissue. When employed to compress an artery and control bleeding, they are called hemostats. Another type of locking forceps is the needle holder, which is used to guide a suturing needle through tissue. Many locking forceps feature finger loops to facilitate handling. These loops are typically held with the thumb and middle or ring fingers, while the index finger helps guide the instrument. The most common locking mechanism involves a series of interlocking teeth located near the finger loops. As the forceps are closed, the teeth engage, preventing the grasping surfaces from separating. A simple shift of the fingers disengages the teeth, allowing the grasping ends to open. Locking forceps are widely used in surgical procedures. Kelly Forceps Kelly forceps are an example of locking forceps, shown in both closed and open positions. They feature a toothed locking mechanism near the finger loops, which secures the instrument during use. Forceps in Childbirth Forceps can also be employed to assist in the delivery of a baby as an alternative to the ventouse method. This application is specific to obstetrics and requires specialized training and expertise.
